name: PT Alamtri Minerals Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Alamtri Minerals Indonesia: a met-coal cash machine whose price now leans on the smelter
frontmatter.summary: We move ADMR to REDUCE from SELL. Two review fixes drive the change: the coal sustaining-capex rate is now D&A-anchored rather than the expansion-year build, and the FY2025 net-debt line is restated to the filing's own reconciliation. The smelter stays at disclosed book value, never zero. The coal business now carries most of the price; the residual gap is the smelter, which we still cannot source earnings for. Target Rp1,058, total return -14.6%.
thesis: The coal business now carries most of the price: the life-of-asset DCF supports US$2,831.9m of enterprise value and, after crediting the smelter at its disclosed book value and releasing its own debt and minority, the primary reads Rp1,109 per share against a price of Rp1,305.

We carry the aluminium smelter at its disclosed book value, never at zero and never at an invented margin: the metal-processing segment shows 1,469 USD m of assets and 977 USD m of liabilities, and AMI's 65.0% share of that net book value is the sourced floor the house card requires for a development project.

The group debt is overwhelmingly the smelter's: KAI's bank loans were 685 USD m of AMI's 713 USD m total interest-bearing debt in the last audited year, so the coal free cash flow is being asked to service capital that built another asset.

The dividend is thin against the capital programme and disappears in the funding case: the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp57 does not rescue a -14.6% total return, and where the coal cash funds the smelter's completion and the interest on the whole stack there is nothing left to pay out.

The two lenses now agree closely rather than fighting by several times: the life-of-asset DCF reads Rp1,109 and the whole-group EV/EBITDA leg Rp1,087 on a 7.7x multiple, with a Rp843 peer-yield leg below both; we believe the primary and carry the other two at their config weights.

The residual gap is the smelter, and it is now modest: today's price needs the benchmark to print US$137/t against the deck's reviewed US$118/t, a factor of 1.2x, and the whole of that premium sits on an aluminium business whose economics no filing has yet shown.

blocks.text: We move **PT Alamtri Minerals Indonesia Tbk** — the metallurgical coal and mineral processing arm of the AlamTri group — to **REDUCE** from SELL, with a target of Rp1,058 against a price of Rp1,305, a total return of -14.6% once the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp57 is included. The coal asset itself is a hard-coking-coal producer with an ultra-low-ash product, a stable strip ratio and an integrated river-to-barge logistics chain, and this refresh makes that coal business carry most of the traded price; the residual gap is the price the market still pays for an aluminium smelter whose earnings no filing has yet shown.

Four things changed in this refresh, and all four are re-underwrites rather than opinion. First, the sustaining-capex rate: the coal business no longer carries the expansion-year build in its capital charge. The last version charged the expansion-year rate against a mine whose infrastructure is now completed, which over-deducted coal cash flow for the whole life of the asset; we now anchor sustaining capital on the restated depreciation the accounts actually take, a rate that also sits at the top of the coal peer set. Second, the FY2025A net-debt line is restated to the filing's own reconciliation — the accounts' cash and interest-bearing-debt lines, not the data pack's wider cash scope — so the model now ties to the audited balance sheet. Third, the smelter is carried at its disclosed net book value rather than at zero, with its own debt and minority released symmetrically. Fourth, the scenario set is mirrored on the two drivers the engine actually prices, with the met-anchored and funding readings carried as named risks in the risks section. The two corrections above move the rating; the smelter floor and the royalty-and-opex fixes of the prior round are unchanged [S2][S0].

Our variant view is narrower than it was, and we state it precisely. The market is paying for the aluminium smelter above what the group has disclosed it is worth. Our primary construction — a life-of-asset discounted cash flow of the coal business at the sector deck's through-cycle marker — is worth US$2,831.9m of enterprise value, which covers the group's post-smelter net debt, the smelter minority charged against it and the smelter at book, leaving the primary at Rp1,109 per share. That is close to the tape but not at it. We do not invent a smelter margin: there is no aluminium revenue, cash cost or segment result to price one from, so the segment's own disclosed net book value is the floor we carry, and the balance of the price above our number is what the market is paying for an earnings stream no filing has yet shown. We are therefore unwilling to underwrite the remaining gap, and we say so plainly.

Three things move the value. First, the metallurgical premium to the deck's benchmark: we calibrate the realised-to-benchmark ratio on the last audited year's actual selling price over that year's benchmark average and hold it flat, so any widening of the coking-coal premium over the thermal marker lifts the target, and any normalisation of Chinese and Mongolian supply compresses it. Second, the smelter: its ramp, its remaining capital programme and its eventual earnings are the single largest unpriced item in the equity, and every quarter that passes without a segment result makes the market's implicit capitalisation of it harder to verify. Third, the funding of the whole programme, because the group's interest-bearing debt more than doubled in the last audited year and the coal free cash flow is what services it. A reader who thinks the smelter is worth the group debt it has consumed should not follow us; a reader who is not paid to take that view is being asked to fund it at today's price [S2].

The Indonesian coal industry has for two decades been a study in converting a depleting,
price-taking resource into a longer-lived industrial business. Families that built thermal
coal franchises have repeatedly used the cash flow of the pit to fund downstream
processing, power, or logistics assets that are meant to outlive the mine. The pattern
carries a structural risk that has nothing to do with the coal price: the industrial
assets consume capital for years before they earn anything, and the coal business is the
only thing generating cash while they do. That is the shape of the business we are
underwriting here, and it is why the balance sheet, not the reserve, is the first thing a
reader should price.

PT Alamtri Minerals Indonesia Tbk is a holding company for two operating pillars: metallurgical coal mining, and mineral processing built around an aluminium smelter. It is a subsidiary of PT Alamtri Resources Indonesia Tbk, which holds 85.0% of the shares, with the balance free-floating; the group sits at the end of a long corporate simplification in which the parent separated its thermal-coal pillar and re-focused on metallurgical coal and downstreaming [S2].

The coal pillar is the cash engine. Through its subsidiaries it holds five Coal Contracts of Work across Central and East Kalimantan — contracts of work, which is the licence basis that fixes how the royalty is charged — and its flagship is Enviromet, a hard coking coal and semi-soft coking coal with ultra-low ash and low phosphorus content — properties that let steelmakers use it with less waste and stronger products, and that earn it a place alongside Australian met coal in the region's coke and steel supply chains. Coal production rose to 7.4 Mt in the last audited year from 6.6 Mt the year before, and sales kept pace, with the company meeting the volume target it had set for itself. The product sells into a concentrated set of Asian buyers: the largest single market in the last audited year was domestic, followed by Japan as the largest export destination at 28.0% of export volumes, then India and China. That mix matters for the pricing model, because the domestic coke plants and the Japanese steel mills buy on met-coal specifications rather than on the thermal marker [S2].

The second pillar is the aluminium smelter, developed by PT Kalimantan Aluminium Industry in an industrial park in North Kalimantan. AMI owns 65.0% of KAI, with the balance held by a non-controlling partner, and the smelter has a nameplate capacity of 500 kt of aluminium ingot a year. It reached partial testing and commissioning at the end of the last audited year and is meant to ramp to full capacity in the following year, positioning the group inside Indonesia's mineral-downstreaming programme and reducing the country's dependence on imported aluminium. It is a genuine strategic asset; it is also, on the disclosures available to us, a pre-revenue one. The segment note shows the metal-processing block with no revenue in the last two audited years and a small loss, 4.6 USD m, which is the signature of a plant in commissioning rather than of a business with an earnings stream we can model [S2].

Strategy, as the board states it, is to use the metallurgical coal cash flow to fund the downstream industrial build and to convert a finite, price-taking resource into longer-lived, contracted industrial demand. The company frames this as participation in the green industrial ecosystem and in the government's downstreaming agenda, and it has spent accordingly: it completed a haul-road upgrade, a second barge-loading conveyor and a large camp at the mine during the last audited year, and it drew bank loans for the smelter at the same time. The execution risk is not in the coal pit, which is running well and at a stable strip ratio; it is in the funding and the timing of the industrial leg, which is where the group's debt has gone and where the equity's value now sits [S2].

ADMR produces metallurgical coal, but the market it trades against is the seaborne coal complex as priced by our sector deck, whose reviewed marker is the Newcastle thermal benchmark. There is no separate reviewed coking-coal series in the deck, so the thermal marker is our through-cycle anchor and the metallurgical premium lives inside the realisation ratio we calibrate on actuals. That is the correct way round for a producer whose realised selling price keys off coking-coal contracts rather than off the thermal tape, but it means the review has to be explicit that the deck's US$118/t is a thermal marker carried as a proxy, and that the met premium is a modelled, measured ratio rather than a deck series [S0].

The demand picture the company paints is a market whose centre of gravity is shifting east. Global crude-steel production fell in the last year, led by cuts in China, Japan and South Korea, while growth momentum moved towards India and South-East Asia; the company argues that Indian infrastructure and housing demand, and new coke-oven capacity across the region, will keep pulling seaborne metallurgical coal even as the traditional markets soften. On the supply side it points to weather disruption and safety inspections in producing provinces that curtailed output through the year. The honest counter-argument is the one we carry in our model: competitively priced alternatives and the normalisation of Chinese and Mongolian supply cap the import appetite, and "capex discipline" theses in this sector fail more often than not once incentive prices are exceeded, because new supply arrives two to four years after a price peak [S2].

Government policy is the second structural force, and it cuts both ways. The state sets a standing domestic price cap for coal sold to the power sector at US$70.0/t, a level far below the seaborne marker, and it sets reference prices for the higher-grade coal products; it also runs a tiered royalty band for the newer IUPK licences, which is not the regime this company pays under. The cap does not bind this company, because its product is metallurgical and sells to steelmakers rather than to power generators — its tonnes are not the domestic power tonnes the cap prices. The royalty does bind it, and it is the single largest deduction from revenue after the cost of the coal itself, but on the licence it actually holds: ADMR's five concessions are Coal Contracts of Work, and the accounts recognise the royalty "arrangements under the CCoWs" as a provision inside cost of revenue rather than as a tax [S2]. Because a contract-of-work royalty is set by the contract rather than by a published schedule, the model carries the flat effective rate the audited accounts actually pay — the same rate in each of the last two audited years — rather than importing the IUPK reference-price band, which would charge this group a materially higher percentage of revenue than its own accounts do [S2]. Alongside the royalty sits the annual production-quota discipline: the ministry approved the great majority of the national work-and-budget plans for the current year against a national coal output of around 720 Mt, a ceiling that keeps the domestic supply backdrop tight even as individual producers jostle for quota [S2][S9].

Competitive position is comfortable but not exceptional. In metallurgical coal the relevant comparisons are the Australian producers and the Mongolian land-borne supply, and ADMR's edge is product specification and logistics rather than scale: an ultra-low-ash, low-phosphorus coking coal, a hauling road that has been chip-sealed for all-weather operation, a second barge-loading conveyor at the river, and a new coal handling and processing plant funded by a bond raised in the current year. That combination is what lets it hold its met specification through the wet season, and it is a real moat against weaker Indonesian met-coal suppliers — but it is a moat around a finite reserve, not around a franchise. The buyer side is highly concentrated, with a handful of steel mills and coke plants in Japan, India, China and Indonesia setting the price, and the supplier side is fragmented among Australian and Mongolian competitors with far larger reserve bases. Regulators hold two powerful levers, the royalty and the production quota, and the logistics chain — a river that runs low in the dry season — is a hard operational constraint the company does not control. That is a business with real cost advantage and weak pricing power: a stable strip ratio at 3.5x, an integrated chain and a specification that holds through the wet season, which is the position worth owning in this industry, and one we would own at the right price. We do not claim a cost-curve quartile for it, because the archived set carries no cash cost per tonne, no all-in sustaining cost and no cost-curve position at all; we rank it on the cost evidence it discloses, and we say so rather than asserting a rank we cannot source [S2].

Our macro frame is stated here because a commodity name cannot be judged outside it. The house tilt carries thermal coal and the commodity bloc as a whole at NEUTRAL with risk appetite at CAUTIOUS, and the war premium in the energy complex is a geopolitics overlay rather than a re-rating case; the through-cycle marker this report re-sets is the metallurgical premium, which the deck does not carry and which therefore lives in our own realisation ratio [S0].

The reported financials tell a clean cyclical story and an unclean capital story. Revenue fell to US$972.9m in the last audited year from a higher level the year before, because realised prices eased even as volumes grew; gross profit fell further, because the cost of revenue barely moved. Our restated D&A is the first correction a reader needs here: the data pack carries a depreciation charge of a fraction of the real number, and we replace it with the audited notes. The depreciation and amortisation line now carries the mining segment's full charge — 44.0 USD m for the last audited year and 37.6 USD m for the year before, both in the pack's reporting currency — and the mining-property amortisation of 15.2 USD m and 13.6 USD m is a component inside that total, not a second addition, so the restatement no longer understates history by the amortisation it claims to add. That total, rather than the fixed-asset charge alone, is what makes the EBITDA in this report larger than the pack's store would suggest [S2].

The balance sheet carries a second correction the reader should be able to trace. The data pack's cash line for the last audited year is a wider scope than the accounts' own: 369 USD m against the 713 USD m of interest-bearing debt the pack also carries, so the model previously read a net debt above the filing's. The accounts publish their own net-debt reconciliation — cash of 369 USD m, interest-bearing debt of 713 USD m and net debt of US$343.9m — and we now restate both lines to it, so the model ties to the audited balance sheet rather than to the data pack's wider cash definition. The forecast income statement then runs the same stack from the filing's own line, so the bridge and the profit and loss account no longer disagree by the cash scope [S2][S0].

The forecast is a volume-led re-rating on a reversionary price. We carry volumes growing modestly from the last actual year as the mine's infrastructure comes on stream and the quota ceiling binds, and a flat realised-to-benchmark ratio calibrated on the last audited year's actual selling price against that year's benchmark average, held flat across the forecast rather than fitted to a forecast-year spike — a ratio fitted to a spike would carry a trough price into the long run. On the deck's reversion path revenue eases from US$1,273.4m towards US$1,198.1m and then holds, with EBITDA easing from US$560.7m and margins compressing as the price path normalises. The royalty is the deduction that has changed most in this refresh, and it is now sourced to the company rather than to a reference band. ADMR holds Coal Contracts of Work, so its royalty is contract-specific and is recognised as a provision inside cost of revenue, not as a charge set by the published IUPK reference-price schedule [S2]. We therefore carry the flat effective rate the filings themselves show — 125 USD m of royalty in the last audited year and 147 USD m the year before it, the same share of revenue in each — and the modelled rate of 12.8% of revenue in the current forecast year is that rate, applied flat across the forecast and the long run. Version one imported the tiered IUPK band, which charged this group a materially higher percentage of revenue than its own accounts take; that overstated the deduction, and correcting it is the largest single reason the coal cash flow in this refresh is higher than in version one [S2].

Costs are anchored on the mine's own disclosures. The strip ratio held at the same level as the prior year at 3.5x, on overburden that rose in line with production, and we carry that ratio flat because no drift is disclosed, while noting the rising overburden as a watch item. Mining cost per bank cubic metre is held at the last audited year's implied rate; the residual other cash cost — haul, barge and process — is set as the figure that reconciles the audited cost of revenue after royalty and restated depreciation, and it covers the river-to-barge logistics chain the company describes. Nothing in the cost base is calibrated off an unchecked depreciation figure; that is why the restatement was done first, and why the cash-cost identity is stated in the assumption file [S2].

Operating expenses are the other cost line this refresh re-bases, and the reason is a definitional one the reader should be able to follow. The operating-expense line the model's history carries is the audited gross-profit-less-operating-income figure, which is the accounts' own operating expenses (43.6 USD m) plus the other-expenses line (33.3 USD m) — not the narrower operating-expense note on its own. Version one carried the narrower note ratio, which is roughly half the line the history uses, so once the royalty was corrected to the contract rate that narrower ratio would have left the first forecast year earning an EBITDA about a tenth above the last audited year. Carrying the last audited year's own ratio instead makes the first forecast year reproduce the last actual year almost exactly, which is what the base case is required to do — and the reader should note precisely what it reproduces: the *consolidated* last audited year, since the line the history carries is the group's, not the mining segment's alone. The perimeter is disclosed rather than hidden: the DCF discounts coal cash flows but the cost base behind them is the group's, the mining segment's own operating cost being a materially smaller share of mining revenue than the group ratio implies. That is a cost the model deliberately over-charges against the coal revenue line, and it is the conservative direction, offsetting the value the same perimeter choice adds elsewhere; the segment restatement is the next item on the worklist and is named as such rather than presented as done. The cost is real and the growth of it — a step-up in employee and professional costs as the mine and the smelter projects were built — is disclosed in the accounts [S2][S3].

Cash flow and the balance sheet are where the story turns. Free cash flow was sharply negative in the last audited year — US$-251.8m — because capital expenditure of US$661.7m was dominated by construction rather than replacement: the coal infrastructure and the smelter. Interest-bearing debt rose to 713 USD m in the last audited year, on bank-loan drawdowns for the smelter, and total liabilities reached 1,170 USD m; the coal business's own borrowings are a small fraction of that, with the smelter's bank loans at 685 USD m of the consolidated total of 713 USD m. The bond raised by the coal subsidiary in the current year, 2,000 IDR bn, is directed mostly to capital expenditure and predominantly to the coal handling and processing plant, so it is coal capital finding a coal use; the smelter's drawdowns are the other story entirely [S2][S5]. We searched the record since the balance-sheet date for anything that belongs in the bridge — a dividend declared, a rights issue, a divestment, an asset held for sale, a material acquisition — and found none; the only post-balance-sheet financing event is the coal subsidiary's own bond, which funds coal capital rather than releasing value, so no bridge item is added [S3][S5][S9].

One debt basis runs through this report, and the reader should be able to reproduce it. The forecast income statement services the same stack the valuation bridge charges: the filing's interest-bearing debt of US$713.0m plus the half-year drawdown of US$1,136.4m gives the US$1,849.4m stack carried from the current year forward, and it is re-costed at 8.0% — the coal subsidiary's own new bond issue rate, well above the pre-drawdown default the engine would otherwise apply — so the bridge and the profit and loss account no longer run two different debt bases against each other. The bridge in the DCF table above prints the net debt and the smelter minority it charges in full [S0][S5].

The earnings-quality screen, run before the thesis, gives four findings. First, accruals: profit attributable to the parent was US$441.0m, US$436.7m and US$271.2m across the last three audited years, while cash from operations fell to 177 USD m in the last of them from 524 USD m the year before, on total assets of 2,891 USD m and 2,074 USD m; accruals turned sharply positive and cash conversion is trending down, so the reported profit is outrunning the cash the business is generating. Second, board and notation status: we found no special-monitoring-board status, no special notation letter and no suspension or delisting event anywhere in the archived record, so the regulator's regime flags do not gate this name. Third, related-party gravity: sales of mining products to related parties ran at 212 USD m in the half-year against 370 USD m to third parties, a substantial transfer-priced share of revenue rather than a market-cleared one. Fourth, structure flags: we checked for pledged controlling stakes, serial rights issues, discounted placements to affiliates, auditor down-tier changes and PSAK 16 revaluation optics and found none disclosed; the single live item, a stated dividend policy subordinated to a debt-funded capital programme, is an optics-class flag rather than a manipulation-class one, and no manipulation-class flag was found [S2][S3].

Our forecast keeps the coal free cash flow clean of the smelter, and this is where the largest correction of this refresh sits. Sustaining capital is charged at the D&A-anchored rate of 7.0 US$/t of sales, equal to the restated depreciation the accounts take and at the top of the coal peer set, rather than at the expansion-year build the prior version carried: the coal handling plant is charged in the current year, and the smelter's own completion spend is excluded precisely because the smelter's revenue is excluded — a coal-only free cash flow is charged with coal-only capital, which is the discipline this model needs to stay honest. Charging the completed haul-road, camp and conveyor build against the coal business for the whole life of the asset was the single largest deduction in the prior version, and removing it is the main reason the coal enterprise value in this refresh is higher. The most important earnings-quality finding is not in the coal numbers at all. It is that earnings are being consumed by a capital programme, that the debt funding it sits on the group balance sheet while the earnings sit in the coal subsidiary, and that the balance sheet has grown far faster than the earnings base it supports — total assets rose while the coal reserve did not. A reader should treat the group's reported profit as a coal profit carrying a smelter financing cost, and price the two separately. The company's own investor page reproduces the same balance-sheet history, which is the right place to check the build [S2][S6].

Two accounting features of Indonesian coal producers are worth flagging for a non-specialist
reader. The first is that local issuers typically present cash-flow statements under the
direct method, which is why the depreciation line in the statement store can be a small
fraction of the real charge taken against the asset base; the fix is to take depreciation
and amortisation from the notes rather than the statement. The second is that a
construction project of this size capitalises its interest into the asset while it is being
built, so the profit reported during the build looks better than the cash economics, and
the reported profit looks worse once the plant starts and the interest lands in the income
statement. Both features are mechanical, and both are the reason the restated figures in
this report differ from the pack's raw store.

Our method set is the house standard for a commodity producer: a life-of-asset discounted cash flow at through-cycle prices as the primary, an EV/EBITDA cross-check against peer medians and the company's own history, and a dividend-yield cross-check, because IDX coal names trade on dividend capacity and the dividend is the market's anchor in this sector. The method fits because the value of the enterprise is dominated by a finite metallurgical reserve whose worth is a function of a price we are not allowed to take from the spot tape, and because a depleting pit has no terminal value — so the DCF is cut at the year that maximises cumulative value rather than grown into perpetuity. The method misfits for exactly one reason, and it is the reason this name is difficult: the listed entity also owns a smelter that is not a coal asset and that this template cannot value [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the deck. The risk-free rate, the mature-market equity premium, the Indonesian country premium, the corporate debt spread and the statutory tax rate come from the macro deck; the unlevered beta is the industry median of the house regressions against the Jakarta index; the debt-to-equity weight is taken from the market's own capitalisation against the group's net debt. The result is a weighted average cost of capital of 10.1% and a cost of equity of 13.0%, at the low end of the range but well inside the house bounds, reflecting a producer with real leverage but a modest equity-risk load [S0].

Here is the central disclosure of this report, stated without euphemism. We value the coal business with a life-of-asset discounted cash flow and we carry the aluminium smelter at its **disclosed book value, and never at zero**. The smelter is not ignored and it is not invented: the company publishes no aluminium smelter revenue, no cash cost per tonne and no margin, so the economics cannot be modelled, but it does publish the metal-processing segment's own balance sheet — 1,469 USD m of assets against 977 USD m of liabilities — and AMI owns 65.0% of the smelter vehicle, whose nameplate is 500 kt. The house method is explicit that a development project is worth at least its sourced sunk capital and never zero, so the smelter enters the model at AMI's attributable share of that net book value, credited across the bridge rows the DCF table prints. That is a floor, not a valuation of the smelter's earnings; when a segment result with a cash cost per tonne exists, it will be re-underwritten. The DCF itself still discounts only the coal cash flows, to an enterprise value of US$2,831.9m — a genuine, sourced number [S2].

The second disclosure is about the debt, and it is now symmetric. The engine bridges from enterprise value to equity using the consolidated balance sheet — the half-year statement at 30 June 2026 — so the coal enterprise value is charged the group's post-smelter net debt and the smelter minority, and the gross stack behind them is US$1,849.4m, the same figure the forecast income statement services. Charging that stack while carrying the smelter at nothing would charge the smelter's own borrowings twice; releasing them is the correction this refresh makes. The bridge therefore credits AMI's share of the smelter's net book value and, in the same construction, releases the smelter's own audited borrowings (KAI's bank loans were 685 USD m of the consolidated 713 USD m in the last audited year, and the current year's further drawdowns finance the same plant) and the minority that belongs to the KAI equity now carried. The release uses the last audited KAI loans, so the H1-2026 drawdowns are under-released and the construction stays conservative on the coal side. The allocation is stated so the reader can apply their own: on a full-smelter-debt allocation the coal equity would read lower, and the DCF table prints the pieces rather than a single opaque charge [S2][S0].

Three inputs do the work in the coal DCF, and all three are stated so the reader can reproduce the number. First, sustaining capital, which this refresh re-anchors: it is charged at 7.0 US$/t of sales, the restated depreciation the accounts actually take and the top of the coal peer set, rather than the expansion-year build the prior version carried. The prior rate was five times the restated depreciation charge and seven to seventeen times the COAL peers the comps table prints, and its source year sat inside a production ramp, so it charged the coal business for capacity the mine had already built and all but exhausted the reserve's value in the model. The corrected rate is the D&A-anchored alternative the review named, and the change is the single largest reason the coal enterprise value in this version is higher than the last [S2]. The realised-to- benchmark ratio is carried flat at 1.43x, calibrated on two consecutive audited actuals rather than fitted to a forecast-year spike, and it is a stated choice rather than an oversight: the deck carries no metallurgical series the engine can read [S0][S2]. The third is the royalty, and it is the one the prior refresh moved: carrying the contract-of-work rate the accounts pay, rather than the IUPK reference band, is the largest single reason this version's coal enterprise value is higher than the first version's [S2].

The published level and the primary now agree closely, and we no longer have to adjudicate a gap of several times. The life-of-asset DCF — the method we believe — reads Rp1,109 per share, the whole-group level multiple reads Rp1,087 at a 25% weight, and the dividend-capacity leg Rp843 at 15%, so the target of Rp1,058 is carried by a set of lenses that sit within a few per cent of one another rather than by a single outlier. The level multiple applies 7.7x to the restated US$360.4m of trailing EBITDA — not the data pack's superseded figure — and that multiple is an average of the sector's own trading multiple and this company's five-year average, both struck while the coal complex carried a war premium; a depleting reserve should not be capitalised on a peer multiple meant for longer-lived assets, which is why we weight the primary. The dividend-yield leg is a re-rating statement: our next-twelve-month dividend capitalised at the peer median yield of 6.8%, giving Rp843 — the softest of the three, because it capitalises a dividend the funding case can cut. Each cross-check does a different job rather than repeating the primary through a shared bridge, and the honest statement is that every lens sits below the price of Rp1,305 by roughly fifteen per cent, that the primary is the highest of them, and that the residual gap is the market's capitalisation of the smelter rather than any dispute about the coal cash flows [S0].

The realised price we carry against a thermal marker is the assumption the archive itself tests, and we name that test rather than burying it. This is a metallurgical producer, but the deck has no coking-coal series, so a met price cannot be an engine driver. The archive does carry one: PLV FOB Australia averaged US$188/t and PLV CFR China US$182/t in the last audited year, against a realised selling price that implies a ratio below the 1.43x we carry on the thermal marker. That is the single largest assumption risk here, and we carry it as a named risk in the risks section rather than as a scenario shock, because the scenario set is required to move the two drivers the engine prices — the benchmark and volume — by mirrored amounts. The honest statement is that a reader who prefers the archive's own coking-coal series should read the thermal-anchored realisation as the generous end of the range; the rating does not change either way, because even the mirrored bear of Rp502 against a base of Rp1,144 leaves no case for the traded price beyond the smelter [S0][S2].

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the residual gap. At today's price the market is implying a benchmark of US$137/t against the deck's reviewed US$118/t — a factor of 1.2x on the reviewed marker, held for the life of the asset, and a far smaller premium than the prior version's. The sensitivity grid is generated from the industry configuration, a manifest-pinned file this desk cannot widen from a company file, so its top step on the benchmark sits below that implied price; we publish the implied benchmark in this text instead, which is the honest way to show a price the grid cannot reach. The decomposition the market is choosing between is now explicit and small. At Rp1,305 the market capitalises IDR53,351.4bn of equity against our coal enterprise value of US$2,831.9m and the smelter at AMI's attributable share of its net book value, the bridge rows the DCF table prints — so the tape is not paying several times the filings, it is paying a modest premium over a coal-only construction, and that premium is the market's own valuation of the aluminium business. On the smelter leg alone, the price above our coal value and the smelter's book is the market's own valuation of the aluminium business: on KAI's ownership that values it on a full-ownership basis at a figure close to its whole disclosed asset base of 1,413 USD m, and per tonne of its nameplate capacity of 500 kt at a level a greenfield aluminium build does not support. That is the bull case, stated with the same construction we use for our own numbers, and it is the case we decline to underwrite until a segment result with a cash cost per tonne exists [S0][S2].

The downside risks are real and we size them honestly. The regulatory risk is the most persistent, and this refresh changes its shape rather than its size. We now carry the contract-of-work rate the accounts pay, which is lower than the published IUPK schedule would be, so the royalty is a risk of re-setting rather than a standing overcharge: when a contract of work is extended or converted, the licence basis — and with it the rate — can be re-cut, and the state has shown it will move coal royalty terms. Beyond the royalty, the production quota is re-won every year, and the domestic price caps, while not binding on metallurgical tonnes today, are a live policy instrument. The macro risk is the steel cycle — Chinese output falling while Indian and South-East Asian demand takes up the slack — plus the currency, which matters because the company earns dollars and the market prices it in rupiah; a weaker rupiah mechanically lifts the target but is a symptom of the balance-of-payments pressure our macro desk currently flags. The commodity risk is the metallurgical premium: our model assumes the premium to the thermal marker holds flat at its last-audited-year level, and a normalisation of Chinese and Mongolian supply would compress it at the same time as the thermal marker reverts, which is a double hit [S2][S9].

The operational risk is the river-to-barge logistics chain. The company ships its coal down the Barito system to the loading points, and it says itself that the hauling-road upgrade was chip-sealed specifically so that navigation and operations continue "under all weather conditions" — an admission that weather is a standing constraint on the chain, not a one-off. Its mitigations are the second barge-loading conveyor at the river, the haul-road upgrade and the coal handling and processing plant now under construction, and they are the right response, but they reduce rather than remove the seasonal exposure to low water. Governance risk is the family control and the related-party flows that come with it, and liquidity risk is the mismatch between a coal business that generates the cash and a smelter that consumes it: net debt to last-audited-year EBITDA reads 1.0x on our restated numbers, but that ratio was struck before the whole drawdown had landed, and it is not the ratio that matters. The two output-contract measures that bind here are the ones the template cannot print from the disclosures: the modelled plan consumes the whole reserve of 178 Mt by the final year of the horizon, so the reserve life is the horizon and the pit closes there, and the closure obligation — 29.0 USD m of non-current provision plus a current portion, with 3.0 USD m charged through cost of revenue in the last audited year — is disclosed in the accounts. It is not inside the discounted window: the life DCF is cut at the year that maximises cumulative value, one year before the reserve is finally exhausted, so the closure outflow is disclosed but sits outside the priced horizon rather than being claimed as a modelled charge. We publish no cost-curve quartile because the archived set contains no cost curve to rank against, which is the same reason we do not claim one in the industry section [S2].

Bear, base and bull now move the same two drivers by mirrored amounts, which is the house rule for a commodity name: the deck's benchmark is re-priced a fifth down in the bear and a fifth up in the bull, and volume is shaded or lifted around the base by the same small margin, so the two tails bracket the base rather than each telling its own story. That gives a bear value of Rp502 against the base of Rp1,144 and a bull of Rp1,441, and the base case still pays a next-twelve-month dividend of Rp57. The two readings we consider the honest downside are carried as named risks rather than as extra shocks, because the scenario gate forbids lopsided tails: the met-anchored reading, in which the archive's own coking-coal series implies a realisation ratio materially below the thermal-anchored premium we carry, and the funding drain, in which the coal cash flow is absorbed by the smelter's completion spending and the interest on the whole debt stack rather than being paid out. A third is the transfer-pricing exposure the related-party share carries: more than a third of the half-year mining revenue went to related parties (212 USD m against 370 USD m), so a five-to-ten per cent haircut to that arm of the realised price is a named downside on the revenue the model calibrates, not a footnote. Both are real, both point the same way as the bear, and a reader who takes them should read the bear tail as the centre. The bull case requires coking-coal supply disruption to persist, the met premium to hold or widen, logistics to normalise and the sales ramp to reach the top of the quota ceiling; on those drivers the bull value of Rp1,441 clears the traded price, which is what a genuine re-rating would need and what this model will only pay if the coking-coal premium widens from here. The trigger that would change our view is not a price move; it is a disclosure event: a first audited metal-processing segment result with a stated cash cost per tonne, which would let us put a sourced number on the smelter and re-underwrite the whole equity. Until that arrives, the signposts we watch are the quarterly shipment and strip-ratio prints, the benchmark path against the deck, the royalty charge as a percentage of revenue, and the group's debt and interest charge as the smelter ramps [S2][S9].

Ownership is concentrated and family-anchored. The parent, PT Alamtri Resources Indonesia Tbk, holds 85.0% of the shares, and the free float is correspondingly small, which is the first thing a reader should notice about liquidity. The parent itself is controlled through a chain of Thohir-family and associate vehicles, and the board of commissioners is chaired by a member of the controlling family; the company also carries independent commissioners, consistent with the regulatory requirement that independent commissioners make up more than a third of the board. The AGMS approves the annual accounts, the use of profit and the appointment of the public accounting firm that audits the consolidated accounts, which is the standard Indonesian governance sequence and gives the shareholder meeting a real, if limited, lever over the accounts [S2].

Related-party flows are material and worth quantifying rather than waving away. In the half-year, sales of mining products to related parties ran at 212 USD m, alongside third-party sales of 370 USD m and a small other-services line — a structure through which the group's own coal moves, and it means the realised price on part of the volume is a transfer price rather than a market-cleared one [S3]. The dividend record is short but real: the company paid 120 USD m in the last audited year, the first distribution since its listing, and it has stated that capital expenditure and debt service come before shareholder returns. We found no evidence of pledged controlling stakes in the disclosures we reviewed, and we note that the auditor and opinion for the audited year are recorded in the annual report even where the extracted text does not name the firm; a reader should verify the opinion letter directly [S2].

On ESG, the company's exposures are the standard ones for an Indonesian coal producer plus one unusual one. The standard exposures are mine rehabilitation and reclamation obligations, which are guaranteed under Indonesian rules and are quantified in the accounts as a provision of 29.0 USD m, charged through cost of revenue at 3.0 USD m in the last audited year — we disclose that obligation and its size rather than treat it as unquantified, though it falls outside the discounted horizon — and the carbon intensity of the product itself, which is the structural headwind on any metallurgical-coal franchise. The unusual exposure is the smelter: the company presents it as part of a lower-carbon industrial transition and as a way to reduce Indonesia's aluminium import dependence, and if the smelter is powered and operated as described it is a genuine diversification away from thermal coal economics. That is a real strategic argument. It is also, on the disclosures available, an argument without numbers, which is precisely why we carry the smelter at its disclosed book value and treat any ESG-driven re-rating of it above that book as unpriced upside rather than as value [S2].

The dated catalysts are the reporting calendar and the smelter's ramp. The third-quarter LK is the first hard test of the river-logistics risk, and it is the print on which the volume build either holds or slips. The full-year production and sales print and the following year's quota awards settle the volume question and therefore the revenue build; the company posts its annual reports and half-year financial statements on its investor site, so the disclosures arrive on a knowable calendar [S7]. The audited accounts are the event that matters most to us, because they carry the first real chance of a metal-processing segment result that would let us value the smelter rather than disclose it. The AGMS decides the dividend and re-appoints the auditor, and the coal subsidiary's bond begins servicing, which is a direct read on whether the coal infrastructure is being funded from coal cash [S2][S5].

Between updates we watch five things. The realised selling price as a percentage of the deck's benchmark, which is our premium and the first casualty of supply normalisation. The shipment and strip-ratio prints, which decide whether the volume plan and the cost base hold. The royalty charge as a percentage of revenue, which is where any re-cutting of the contract-of-work rate would land. The group's net debt and interest expense as the smelter ramps, since that is the charge that sets the residual gap between our coal value and the traded price. And any smelter disclosure with a cash cost per tonne, which is the single item that would move this rating. Until one of those changes, the arithmetic we have shown stands, and the answer it gives is a REDUCE [S2][S5].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2025A sales were 6.28 Mt on production of 7.41 Mt (S2), up from 5.62 Mt in FY2024 (S2); management met its FY2025 5.6-6.1 Mt sales target (S2). H1-2026 revenue rose 31.5% yoy on solid operations (S3), so FY2026E is lifted only to 6.5 Mt, still below the 7.41 Mt produced in FY2025; the ramp thereafter follows the MC capacity build toward the level the RKAB ceiling supports, while the national ~720 Mt RKAB 2026 discipline (S9) constrains the industry backdrop. No low-water or logistics constraint is asserted here: the archived record the report stands behind carries none (round 1: the earlier Barito-drought driver text was dropped, since the low-water material lived only in the discarded source).

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on FY2025A actuals per the desk rule, flat across the forecast, never fitted to a forecast-year spike. FY2025A revenue of 972.948 (S0) over 6.28 Mt sales (S2) gives a realised ASP of ~154.9 US$/t against the deck's FY2025A newc average of 108.4 (reviewed), a ratio of 1.429; FY2024A gives 1.509 (205.4 realised on 136.1), so two consecutive actuals bracket a through-cycle met-coal premium. Anchoring to a thermal marker rather than a met price is a stated choice, not an oversight: the deck carries NO met series (the only coal prices are newc and the HBA/ICI thermal grades, and ici3/ici4 are needs_source), and the engine can only price off a deck series, so a met price cannot be a driver. The archive does name a met series - PLV FOB Australia ~188 US$/t and PLV CFR China ~182 US$/t for 2025 (S2, F39/F40) - and against FY2025A realised of ~154.9 that implies ~0.82x PLV, below our thermal-anchored 1.43. The base case keeps the two-actual thermal-anchored ratio. The PLV-anchored reading is carried as a NAMED DOWNSIDE RISK in section 5, not as a scenario shock: the engine's scenario gate (fund record, scenario.mirror / scenario.symmetry) requires the two tails to shock the SAME drivers by mirrored amounts, so a bear-only realisation cut to 0.5734x would force a mirrored bull at 1.7439x - a met premium more than double the last actual, which the house card's no-unsourced-drift rule forbids. Round 1 responded to this by mis-describing the shocks (the basis text claimed the bear set realisation to 0.82 when it never did); that text is corrected here and section 4 publishes the reading as arithmetic instead. Applied flat at 1.43 including lt: it carries a measured premium, claims no widening into the reversion path, and mirrors sibling ADRO's published met read of 1.42 without copying it.

challenges.challenge: The smelter is carried at zero in the primary and in every scenario, while the DCF bridge charges the group's consolidated net debt of 1,334.338 (gross 1,849.374 less cash 515.036, latest_bs 2026-06-30, fund record) and the KAI minority of 154.627 against a coal-only EV of 680.112394, manufacturing equity of -808.852606 floored at Rp0. The MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE card is explicit that development projects are worth at least their sourced sunk capex and never zero. The zero is caution, not the most-likely read, and it sets 60% of the published target.
challenges.answer: KAI is no longer carried at zero. The DCF bridge now credits AMI 65% of the metal-processing segment net book value (assets 1,468.934 less liabilities 976.860 = 492.074; 65% = 319.848) and, in the same symmetric construction, releases the smelter own audited bank loans (685.010) and the minority it belongs to (154.627), so the smelter debt is not double-charged. Net bridge +1,159.485; primary now 155.4/share (was floored at 0) and the target 535.0, TR -54.6%: still SELL, at a materially higher level, as the red team said it would be.

challenges.challenge: The DCF is labelled coal-only but its costs are consolidated. Note 39 (S2) puts mining-segment FY2025A opex at 31,293 (3.2% of mining revenue 968,800) and other net at -1,754, while the metal-processing leg carries 14,481 of opex plus 7,152 of other income and the corporate leg carries 15,022 of opex plus -32,335 of other net; the model's opex ratio of 8.11% charges all of it against coal revenue. Mining-segment EBITDA is therefore roughly 405m (361.2 plus 44.038 F6) against the model's consolidated 360.437, so the coal-only EV of 680.1 is understated on the cost line by about 45m a year before any other assumption.
challenges.answer: Corrected: the calibration reproduces the CONSOLIDATED last actual, not a coal-only one, and the claim that FY2026E reproduces the coal last actual was false. Section 3 now discloses the perimeter (group cost base charged against coal revenue, the mining segment cost a materially smaller share of mining revenue) and names the segment restatement as the open worklist item rather than asserting it done. The restatement itself is not yet in the model and is reported as an open item.

challenges.challenge: Sustaining capex of 35/t flat to FY2050E is 5x the restated D&A of 7.0/t and 7-17x the COAL peers (AADI 5, BUMI 2, fund record comps), on a reserve the report says is depleting with no terminal value. Its source is FY2023's ~30/t (134.016 of the S2 five-year series 11.3/21.1/134.0/405.7/661.7 over 4.46 Mt sales), an expansion year in a 5.11-to-7.41 Mt production ramp, with no evidence that year was sustaining-only; FY2023 itself included haul-road, conveyor and camp works the 35/t uplift claims to add. Charging 255.5m a year of sustaining capex against ~51m of D&A for 25 years is replacement without replacement reserves.
challenges.answer: Accepted with a model change (QC round 1). The sustaining rate is now the D&A-anchored 7.0 US$/t the LK supports (F6 44.038/6.28 Mt; F7 37.571/5.62 Mt), not 35/t: the FY2025 capex of 661.655 is KAI smelter construction plus the completed MC infrastructure build and FY2023 ~30/t sat inside a 5.11-7.41 Mt expansion ramp, so neither is a sustaining-only read, and the peer set is AADI 5 / BUMI 2. The change clears the capex.long_run gate and lifts the target.

challenges.challenge: Both of the report's named downside readings have dropped out of the priced model. The realisation basis (assumptions line 75-77) still says the bear sets realisation to the PLV-anchored 0.82x, but the current bear shocks are only newc x0.8 and volume x0.95 with realisation flat at 1.43, so no PLV-anchored value is published anywhere in the current numbers.
